title: MFA and stopping guessers
summary: Second factors, how authenticator-app codes (TOTP) work, and throttling attackers who guess passwords online.

steps.title: Multi-factor authentication
body: Passwords get phished, reused and guessed. A second factor means a stolen password alone is not enough.
Common second factors, weakest first:
- **SMS codes**: better than nothing, but SIM-swap attacks and interception make them weak.
- **TOTP codes** from an authenticator app: a 6-digit code that changes every 30 seconds, computed on the phone from a shared secret.
- **Push approval**: "Is this you signing in?" on a phone. Attackers spam requests until a tired user taps yes (**MFA fatigue**), so good apps make you type a number shown on screen.

- **Passkeys / FIDO2 security keys** (WebAuthn): the device signs a challenge with a private key that never leaves it, and the signature is bound to the website's real domain. A fake site gets nothing useful. This is **phishing-resistant**.
A code you can *type* can also be typed into a convincing fake site, which forwards it to the real one within its 30 seconds. Passkeys can't be relayed that way.

steps.prompt: Can each one be captured by a fake login page and replayed to the real site?
steps.explain: Passkeys and FIDO2 keys sign a challenge that includes the site's origin. A phishing domain gets a signature that is worthless on the real domain.

steps.title: How a TOTP code is made
body: TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password, RFC 6238) is short enough to write yourself. The server and the phone share a random secret (that is what the QR code contains). Both compute:
```csharp fragment
long counter = unixSeconds / 30;                 // which 30-second window
byte[] msg = BitConverter.GetBytes(counter);     // 8 bytes
if (BitConverter.IsLittleEndian) Array.Reverse(msg);  // big-endian, as the RFC says
byte[] h = HMACSHA1.HashData(secret, msg);       // 20 bytes
int offset = h[^1] & 0x0F;                       // "dynamic truncation"
int binary = (h[offset] & 0x7F) << 24 | h[offset + 1] << 16
| h[offset + 2] << 8 | h[offset + 3];
int code = binary % 1_000_000;                   // 6 digits

Then format with leading zeros: `code.ToString("D6")`. Because the code depends only on the secret and the clock, phone and server agree without talking. (HMAC is a keyed hash; the JWT module uses it again.)
Servers usually accept the previous and next window too, to allow for clock drift, and remember the last counter used so a code can't be replayed.

steps.prompt: Which 30-second window is each moment in? What does this print?
steps.explain: Integer division groups the seconds into windows of 30. Everyone whose clock reads within the same window computes the same code.
The low 4 bits of the last byte choose where to read; the top bit is masked off so the number is positive; the four bytes are combined big-endian; `D6` keeps leading zeros.

steps.title: Compute a TOTP code
prompt: Write `string Totp(byte[] secret, long unixSeconds, int digits)` following RFC 6238 with HMAC-SHA1 and a 30-second step.
The RFC's own test vectors (secret is the ASCII text `12345678901234567890`, 8 digits):
With `digits = 6`, time 59 gives `287082`. Note the leading zero in `07081804`.
starter: string Totp(byte[] secret, long unixSeconds, int digits)
solution: string Totp(byte[] secret, long unixSeconds, int digits)
hints: Build the 8-byte big-endian counter, then `HMACSHA1.HashData(secret, msg)`.
Truncate as on the card, then `% (int)Math.Pow(10, digits)`.
Format with `ToString("D" + digits)` so leading zeros stay.
template: Dojo.Eq("Totp(key, 1111111109, 8) keeps its leading zero", "07081804", Totp(dojoKey, 1111111109, 8));
Dojo.Eq("Totp(key, 30, 6) is in the same window as 59", Totp(dojoKey, 59, 6), Totp(dojoKey, 30, 6));

steps.title: Brute force and how to slow it
body: Slow hashing protects a *stolen* database. Attackers who guess against your **live login endpoint** need different defences.
- **Brute force**: many passwords against one account.
- **Password spraying**: one common password (`Summer2026!`) against many accounts, staying under per-account limits.
- **Credential stuffing**: username/password pairs leaked from *other* sites, replayed against yours. Very effective, because people reuse passwords.
Defences, used together:
- **Throttle per account and per IP**: after N failures in a window, refuse or delay further attempts. `429 Too Many Requests` with a `Retry-After` header is the HTTP way to say so.
- **Prefer temporary lockouts and growing delays** to permanent lockout. A permanent lock lets anyone lock your users out on purpose (a denial of service).
- **Reject known-breached passwords** at registration (services like Have I Been Pwned offer this).
- **MFA**, which makes a correct password insufficient.
- **Monitor**: many failures across many accounts from a few IPs is spraying or stuffing.
ASP.NET Core ships a rate limiter (`builder.Services.AddRateLimiter`, with fixed window, sliding window and token bucket policies) for per-endpoint limits.

steps.prompt: An attacker tries the password `Winter2026!` once against each of 50,000 accounts. Which defence helps **least**?
options: Locking an account after 5 failed attempts on that account
Rate limiting failed logins per source IP
Rejecting common and breached passwords at sign-up
steps.explain: That is password spraying: each account sees only one failure, so a per-account limit never triggers. Limits across accounts (per IP, global anomaly detection), banning common passwords and MFA all help.

steps.title: A login throttle
prompt: Write a class `LoginThrottle` that tracks failed logins per username and locks an account for a while after too many.
- `void RecordSuccess(string user)`: clears that user's failures.

- `bool IsLocked(string user, DateTimeOffset now)`: `true` when the user has at least `maxFailures` failures whose time is within `window` before `now` (a failure at time `t` counts while `now - t < window`).
The time is passed in, never read from the clock, so the class is easy to test and behaves the same every run.
t.IsLocked("ada", start.AddMinutes(16))          // false: the first failure has aged out
starter: public void RecordFailure(string user, DateTimeOffset now) { }
public bool IsLocked(string user, DateTimeOffset now) => false;
solution: public void RecordFailure(string user, DateTimeOffset now)
public bool IsLocked(string user, DateTimeOffset now) =>
_failures.TryGetValue(user, out var list) && list.Count(t => now - t < _window) >= _max;
hints: Keep a `Dictionary<string, List<DateTimeOffset>>` of failure times.
`IsLocked` counts the failures with `now - t < window`.
template: Dojo.Eq("a new user is not locked", false, dojoT.IsLocked("ada", dojoStart));
Dojo.Eq("2 failures of 3 allowed: not locked", false, dojoT.IsLocked("ada", dojoStart.AddMinutes(2)));
Dojo.Eq("3 failures within 15 minutes: locked", true, dojoT.IsLocked("ada", dojoStart.AddMinutes(3)));
Dojo.Eq("another user is not affected", false, dojoT.IsLocked("grace", dojoStart.AddMinutes(3)));
Dojo.Eq("at exactly 15 minutes the first failure no longer counts", false, dojoT.IsLocked("ada", dojoStart.AddMinutes(15)));
Dojo.Eq("after 16 minutes: unlocked", false, dojoT.IsLocked("ada", dojoStart.AddMinutes(16)));
Dojo.Eq("three new failures inside the window lock it again", true, dojoT.IsLocked("ada", dojoStart.AddMinutes(16)));
Dojo.Eq("a success clears the failures", false, dojoT.IsLocked("ada", dojoStart.AddMinutes(16)));
